newsitem.title: FRANCE: France Telecom sale effectively suspended.
newsitem.headline: France Telecom sale effectively suspended.

text.p: France's biggest ever privatisation, the sale of a minority stake in France Telecom, was effectively suspended on Tuesday awaiting a decision by the new left-wing government.
"Effectively, the Initial Public Offering has been suspended until the new government takes a decision," a France Telecom spokesman said.
He declined to comment whether France Telecom chairman Michel Bon would seek urgent talks with Prime Minister Lionel Jospin or his ministers to argue in favour of the sale.
The spokesman also declined to comment on whether Bon would resign if the sale were definitively cancelled.
He did say that a consultation of France Telecom staff, an idea Jospin launched during the election campaign, could be done rather swiftly.

"Everything is possible. It all depends on the new government and at the moment there is not yet a new government," the spokesman said. "The opening of our capital has been suspended until a decision by the new government, our 100 percent shareholder," he added.

The sale of a 30 to 35 percent stake in France Telecom, which was valued at between 160 and 210 billion francs, had been suspended for four weeks by former Finance Minister Jean Arthuis after President Jacques Chirac called early parliamentary elections on April 22.

Had the centre-right won the election, the sale would have resumed on June 5 with a three week period during which French private investors would have been able to reserve shares ahead of the Initial Public Offer (IPO) with a listing in Paris and New York in early July.
An advertising campaign aimed at drumming up interest for the share has been put on ice.
Financial analysts still believe that a sale of a minority stake will happen but in September at the earliest.

Socialist party spokesmen said during the election campaign that France Telecom would not be privatised but some held the option open that a minority stake could be sold, if only for the 30 to 50 billion francs in revenues it could bring in.
Jospin said that he would consult France Telecom staff, but added the decision was up to the government.
The Communist Party, which is set to claim posts in the new government because the Socialists and ecologists do not have enough seats for a majority, is squarily against any sale of state assets.

Nicole Notat, the moderate leader of France's traditionally Socialist-leaning CFDT union, said on Tuesday she was not hostile to an opening up of France Telecom capital to private investors as long as the state guarnteed a quality public service.
Louis Viannet, the leader of the Communist CGT union said the sale had to be halted and looked at afresh.

"Let's halt it and re-examine the case. Privatisation of France Telecom has nothing to do with the need to develop the sector and would be bad news for the country's assets," he told France Inter radio.
